Anime & manga · Spoiler-light guide · 10 min read

Jujutsu Kaisen begins with a monster’s finger. That is not what makes it frightening.

A teenager swallows a cursed relic and becomes the vessel of an ancient killer. The hook is outrageous. The reason millions stay is more human: in this world, fear and regret do not remain inside us. They take shape.

Researched and edited in Japan by Yuji Shimizu · Published October 12, 2026, 2:15 p.m. JST
Spoiler guide: This feature explains the premise, early character relationships and themes. It names later anime arcs but does not reveal the manga’s final outcome or major deaths.

Yuji Itadori is unusually strong, but strength is not what sets his story in motion. At school in Sendai, he chooses an occult club because it lets him visit his dying grandfather. The old man leaves him with a simple responsibility: use your strength to help people, and do not die alone. Within hours, that moral instruction becomes impossible.

Yuji’s friends unwrap a preserved finger. It belongs to Ryomen Sukuna, a legendary figure feared as the King of Curses. The relic attracts creatures born from human negativity. To save the people around him, Yuji swallows it. Instead of disappearing, Sukuna awakens inside him.

The authorities of the hidden jujutsu world make a brutal calculation. Yuji must eventually be executed, but his rare ability to contain Sukuna offers one delay: find and consume the other fingers, then kill the vessel and erase the threat with him. Satoru Gojo, the dazzlingly powerful teacher who discovers Yuji, brings him to Tokyo Jujutsu High. There he trains beside Megumi Fushiguro and Nobara Kugisaki to fight curses while living under a postponed death sentence.

That is the cleanest description of the plot. It sounds like a supernatural school adventure with an enemy sealed inside the hero. Jujutsu Kaisen quickly refuses the safety of that arrangement. Sukuna is not a gruff inner mentor. The institutions protecting society are not necessarily humane. Victory can leave a wound that does not close when the episode ends.

2018–24Gege Akutami’s original manga ran in Weekly Shonen Jump for six and a half years.
30Main-series collected volumes; Volume 30 is the finale.
100m+Copies in circulation, including digital editions, announced at the September 2024 conclusion.

What does “Jujutsu Kaisen” mean?

The official English title keeps the Japanese words because a literal translation loses the texture. Jujutsu (呪術) means curse techniques or sorcery: 呪 carries the idea of a curse, while 術 is an art, method or technique. Kaisen is written 廻戦, an unusual compound suggesting a circling or revolving battle. The title is less a neat sentence than a charged label: a war in which curses keep turning back through people.

In the story, ordinary humans leak juryoku—cursed energy—from fear, anger, humiliation and grief. Accumulated negativity produces jurei, cursed spirits. Sorcerers learn to control the same energy and channel it into inherited or individual techniques. The fighters therefore use the substance that creates their enemies.

This is the first reason the world feels coherent. The monsters are not visitors from another planet. They are social exhaust. A school, hospital or station can gather fear because people repeatedly bring intense emotions there. The city does not merely provide a dramatic backdrop; crowded human life manufactures the supernatural pressure.

The frightening idea is not that monsters hide among people. It is that people make the monsters, continuously and unintentionally—and the heroes can fight them only by mastering the same darkness.

Why the characters feel dangerous to love

Yuji enters battle with an instinct to save everyone. The story tests whether that desire is morally serious or merely comforting. He is physically gifted, emotionally open and often funny, yet the harm done through his body makes innocence impossible. His central question is not “How do I become the strongest?” It is “What counts as a proper death, and who has the right to decide?”

Megumi Fushiguro offers a colder answer. He does not pretend that everybody can be saved equally; he chooses people he believes deserve help. Nobara Kugisaki refuses the common role of supportive heroine. She likes beauty, shopping and her own ferocity without treating those qualities as contradictions. Their friendship works because the trio are not three parts of one personality. They disagree about the value of a life.

Then there is Gojo. His blindfold, jokes and impossible confidence made him the series’ most instantly recognizable figure, but his narrative function is sharper than charisma. If one person is overwhelmingly strong, an entire society can postpone reform and depend on him. Gojo wants to educate allies who can change the conservative jujutsu establishment. The more powerful he appears, the more the story asks what happens when a system rests on a single human pillar.

Sukuna completes the trap. Many series turn the demon inside the hero into usable power or eventual friendship. Sukuna keeps his own desires. Every moment in which Yuji needs him creates suspense because help may be worse than refusal. The shared body is not a shortcut to strength; it is an occupation.

The combat system turns personality into architecture

Cursed techniques can be intricate, sometimes demanding careful rereading. They also externalize character. Megumi’s shikigami are summoned through shadows. Nobara attacks relationships between a body and a separated piece through straw-doll technique. Gojo manipulates the concept of infinity. The abilities are not interchangeable colored blasts; their conditions expose how each fighter imagines distance, identity, risk and control.

A Domain Expansion pushes that logic furthest. A sorcerer projects an innate domain outward, enclosing opponents in an environment where the user’s technique gains overwhelming force. Visually, a domain can feel like someone’s interior world made into a room. Battles become clashes of interpretation as well as speed.

Restrictions matter. Binding vows exchange freedom or safety for power. Explaining a technique to an opponent may strengthen it because disclosure increases risk. This lets fights reward attention: what a character sacrifices can matter more than the size of an attack.

Cursed energyNegative emotion becomes the power source. Control, not emotional purity, separates sorcerers from ordinary people.
Binding vowA chosen restriction can produce an advantage. Power comes with a legible price.
Domain ExpansionAn inner world becomes a combat space. Psychology turns into architecture.

It moves like spectacle, but remembers consequence

MAPPA’s anime gives the battles weight through choreography, compositing and sharply changing visual styles. The first television season aired from October 2020 to March 2021. The film Jujutsu Kaisen 0, adapted from Akutami’s earlier four-chapter story, followed in 2021. The official film site reports approximately ¥13.8 billion at Japan’s box office and about ¥26.5 billion worldwide.

The second season, broadcast in 2023, moves from Gojo and Suguru Geto’s youth into the Shibuya Incident. The contrast explains much of the series’ emotional design: light, friendship and possibility are not filler before darkness. They establish what later events cost.

Season three’s first half, the Culling Game, aired in Japan from January 8 through March 26, 2026, ending with episode 59. The official Shonen Jump page now lists season four, the second half of the Culling Game, as in production. That current anime momentum is one reason the completed manga remains culturally active rather than sealed in the past.

Why does it pull people in?

First, it respects speed. Akutami can introduce a rule, a joke and a threat in a few pages. The anime translates that momentum into abrupt impact and elastic movement. But speed alone would make the series disposable. The crucial scenes slow down around choices: whom to save, whether a death had meaning, what responsibility survives failure.

Second, the work makes coolness unstable. Gojo can dominate a room and still fail to repair the structure around him. A technique can be beautiful and horrifying. A villain can articulate a philosophical pressure without becoming correct. Fans receive memorable poses and quotable concepts, then discover that style offers no immunity from consequence.

Third, relationships change the meaning of earlier scenes. The prequel film is a clear example. Jujutsu Kaisen 0 follows Yuta Okkotsu and Rika, connecting love, grief and curse in a more self-contained story. Watching it after season one gives useful context; revisiting it after season two makes several bonds feel different. The franchise rewards return journeys rather than only forward momentum.

Finally, its darkness is social. Adults send teenagers into lethal work. Elite families preserve inherited power. Leaders protect procedure while individuals absorb the cost. The series does not present a policy program, but its supernatural bureaucracy feels recognizable: institutions can describe sacrifice as necessity long after they stop asking whether the structure should change.

Where should a beginner start?

  1. Start with TV season one. Its 24 episodes teach the cast and power system in the intended dramatic rhythm.
  2. Watch Jujutsu Kaisen 0 next. It is a prequel centered on Yuta. It can work as a first taste, but season one makes its supporting cast more meaningful.
  3. Continue to season two: Hidden Inventory / Premature Death, then the Shibuya Incident.
  4. Move to season three: the first half of the Culling Game, broadcast in 2026.
  5. Read officially. VIZ publishes the English manga, and MANGA Plus by Shueisha provides official chapter access by region. The main story ends in Volume 30.

Availability differs by country. The anime’s official Japanese site lists current domestic services; check the licensed service in your region rather than an unofficial upload.

One alternative is to begin with Volume 0 or its film. It introduces Yuta and offers a complete emotional arc, but it was created before the main serialization and some concepts feel less settled. Starting with season one preserves Yuji as the doorway; starting with 0 makes the world’s central idea—love can become a curse—immediately clear.

A warning before you enter

This is not light viewing simply because its leads are teenagers. The series depicts graphic injury, body horror, cruelty, mass violence and grief. It can be funny and warm, but it does not promise that affection protects a character. Viewers looking for a stable school-team adventure may find its later arcs punishing.

The rules can also become dense. Some fights depend on translated explanations of techniques, probability or conditions. Confusion is not always your fault; characters themselves sometimes encounter abilities without complete information. Pausing or rereading is part of the experience for many fans.

As of October 12, 2026, the original manga is complete, the anime has adapted through the first half of the Culling Game, and a fourth season is in production. An official sequel, Jujutsu Kaisen Modulo, created by Gege Akutami with art by Yuji Iwasaki, has also completed its run on MANGA Plus. New readers do not need it to understand Yuji’s story; finish the original first.

The word at the center

Noroi (呪い) means “curse.” It can describe supernatural harm, but Japanese also uses it figuratively for something that binds or haunts a person. The verb is norou, to curse. Jujutsu Kaisen keeps asking where a curse begins: in hatred, in love that refuses to release someone, in a family role, or in the demand to give death a proper meaning.

That is why the first finger is only the doorway. The object is grotesque and unforgettable, but the lasting horror is invisible before it becomes a monster. Everyone carries fear. Everyone loses people. The series gives those facts bodies, names and techniques—and then asks whether the same feelings that create curses can also create reasons to keep living.
